## Auto-regressive hidden Markov model

Let xt denote the six-dimensional vector of nose-head-body coordinates at video frame t (sampled at 80 Hz), with components (xnose,ynose,xhead,yhead,xbody,ybody). We fit an AR-HMM to mouse trajectory data, {xti}, across trials (indexed by i) from 13 out of 15 mice (two mice were excluded a priori due to low task performance). These mice performed olfactory search under the following experimental conditions: Variable ΔC, Constant |C| (nine mice); naris occlusion (seven mice); and Constant ΔC, Variable |C| experiments (five mice).

## The generative view

Viewed as a generative model (that generates simulated data), the AR-HMM has two 'layers': a layer of hidden discrete states (corresponding to discrete movement motifs) and an observed layer that is the continuous trajectory xt. We denote the temporal sequence of discrete states by zt. In each time step, zt∈{1,2,…,S}, that is, it is one of an S number of states, or movement motifs. The discrete hidden states evolve in time according to a Markov chain: going from time step t to t + 1, the discrete state may change to another state according to a transition probability matrix πz1,z2, which denotes the conditional probability of switching to z2 having started in z1. The probability distribution over the initial state, zt=1, of the Markov chain at the start of each trial was taken to be the uniform distribution.

Now suppose for time steps t1 to t2 (inclusive) the discrete layer remained in state z. The continuous or auto-regressive (AR) part of the model dictates that, over this time interval, the continuous trajectory, xt, evolves according to a linear AR process. The parameters of this AR process can be different in different states or motifs, z. In other words, xt is governed by(1)xt=Azxt−1+bz+εt.t1≤t≤t2where Az is a 6 × 6 matrix and b is a 6 × 1 vector, and the noise vector εt is sampled from the multi-variate zero-mean Gaussian distribution N0,Qz, where Qz is a 6 × 6 noise covariance matrix. Moreover, the parameters Az, bz, and Qz depend on the discrete state z, and in general are different in different discrete states. The simple stochastic linear dynamics described by Equation (1) can describe simple motions of the mouse, such as turning left/right, dashing towards a certain direction, freezing (when Az is the identity matrix and bz is zero), etc. The switches between these simple behaviors allow the model to generate complex trajectories.

The AR-HMM is an example of a model with latent variables, which in this case are the discrete state sequence zti in each trial. The model, as a whole, is specified by the set of parameters (π,{Az},{bz},{Qz}), which we will denote by θ. For a d-dimensional trajectory (d = 6 here) and S states, comprises SS-1+Sd2+d+dd+1/2=SS-1+3dd+1/2 parameters.

## Model fits

Models with latent variables are often fit using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, which maximizes the likelihood of the model in terms of the parameters θ≡π,{Az},{bz},{Qz} for a given set of observed data {xti}. In this work, we did not use the EM algorithm, but adopted a fully Bayesian approach in which both the hidden variables and the model parameters were inferred by drawing samples from their posterior distribution (Wiltschko et al., 2015). The posterior distribution combines the model likelihood and Bayesian priors imposed on its parameters, according to Bayes' rule. If we denote the joint likelihood of observed trajectories, {xti}, and the latent variables, {zti}, by P{xti,zti}θ and the prior distribution over model parameters by Pθ, then up to normalization, the joint posterior distribution of latent variables and model parameters is given by(2)P{zti},θ{xti}∝P{xti,zti}θPθ.

For the AR-HMM, the (logarithm of the) joint log-likelihood is given by(3)log⁡P{xti,zti}θ=∑i∑t=2Ti[log⁡πzt-1i,zti+logNxtiAztixt-1i+bzti,Qzti].where Ti is the length of trial i, and we use the notation Nxμ,Q=e-12x-μTQ-1x-μ/2πQ to denote the density at point x of a multivariate Gaussian with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Q.

We imposed loose conjugate priors on the model parameters, which were factorized over the parameters of the AR process, {Az},{bz},{Qz}, in different discrete states z, and the different rows of the Markov transition matrix, π. On the rows of π, we imposed Dirichlet distribution priors with uniform distribution means and concentration hyperparameter α, which was set to 4. We imposed matrix normal inverse Wishart priors on the AR parameters, independently for different discrete states. Under this prior, the noise covariance Qz has an inverse Wishart distribution with a 'scale matrix' hyperparameter, which was set to the d × d ( = 6 × 6) identity matrix, and a 'degrees-of-freedom' scalar hyperparameter set to d + 2 = 8. Conditional on Qz, the remaining AR parameters, Az,bz, have a joint multivariate normal distribution under the prior, which can be specified by the prior mean and joint prior covariance matrix of Az and bz. The prior means of Az and bz were set to the d × d identity matrix and the d-dimensional zero vector, respectively, while the prior covariance matrix of the concatenation Az,bz was given by the tensor product of Qz and the (d + 1) × (d + 1)( = 7 × 7) identity matrix (equivalently, under this prior, bz and different columns of Az are independent and uncorrelated, while each of these column vectors has a prior covariance equal to the [prior] AR noise covariance, Qz).

Bayesian model inference was carried out by sampling from (instead of maximizing) the joint posterior distribution of the model parameters and latent state variables conditioned on the observed trajectory data (Equation 2). We did this by Gibbs sampling (an example of Markov chain Monte Carlo; not to be confused with the Markov chain in the AR-HMM), which works in a manner conceptually similar to the EM algorithm: it switches between sampling zti in all trials, conditioned on previously sampled parameters, and then sampling the parameters θ given the previous sample of {zti}. To carry out this model inference procedure, we used the Python package developed by M.J. Johnson and colleagues, publicly available at https://github.com/mattjj/pyhsmm (Johnson et al., 2013a).

We ran the Gibbs sampler for 300 iterations and burned the first 200 samples, retaining 100. We used the remaining samples to obtain the posterior probabilities of hidden discrete states at each time step of each trial (by calculating the frequency of different state in that time step and trial, across the retained Gibbs samples), as well as posterior expectation of the model parameters (by calculating their averages over the retained Gibbs samples). We refer to the AR-HMM with parameters given by these latter posterior expectations as the ‘fit model’.

## Model selection

We fit AR-HMM's with different numbers of states (motifs), S, to mouse trajectory data pooled across animals. To evaluate the statistical goodness of fit of these fit model and select the best S (the number of states or motifs), we evaluated the log-likelihoods of fit models on trajectory data from a held-out set of trials, not used for model fitting. The corresponding plot of log-likelihoods is shown in Figure 6F. As seen, the log-likelihood keeps increasing with S, up to S = 100. This shows that, up to at least S = 100, additional motifs do have utility in capturing more variability in mouse trajectories. These variabilities may include differences in movement across mice, as well as movement variations in the same mouse but across different trials or different instances of the same movement; for example, a clockwise head turn executed with different speeds in different instances or trials. In the AR-HMM, the AR observation distribution of a given Markov state corresponds to a very simple (linear) dynamical system that cannot capture many natural and continuous variations in movement, such as changes in movement speed. Nevertheless, AR-HMM models with higher S can capture such variations with more precision by specializing different discrete Markov states, with different AR distributions, to movement motifs of different mice, or, for example, to capture different speeds of the same qualitative movement motif.

The goal for this modeling was to give a compact description of recurring movement features across animals and conditions, suitable for visualization and alignment. For these purposes, the goodness of fit did not provide a suitable criterion because the log-likelihood plots did not peak or plateau even at very large numbers of states. Guided by visual inspection, we thus chose the model with S = 16 for the main figures (Figures 6–8). Although this was a somewhat arbitrary choice, we show that the findings in Figures 6–8 do not depend on the choice of S – models with S = 6, 10, or 20 gave equivalent results (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4).

## MAP sequences

The Gibbs sampling algorithm that we used for model inference yields (time-wise marginal) maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates of the latent variables {zti}, as follows. Using the Gibbs samples for the latent variables, we can estimate the posterior probability of the mouse being in any of the S states in any given time step of a given trial. We made MAP sequences by picking, at any time step and trial, the state with the highest posterior probability. The inferred MAP motifs tended to have high posterior probability, which exceeded 0.8 in 66.2% of all time steps across the 17,195 trials in the modeled dataset.

## Decoding analysis

We decoded experimental conditions and animal identities from single-trial MAP motif sequences inferred using the AR-HMM. Specifically, we trained multi-class decoders with linear decision boundaries (linear discriminant analysis) to decode the above categorical variables from the single-trial empirical state transition probability matrices derived from the MAP sequence of each trial. If zt(i)^ is the motif MAP sequence for trial i, the empirical transition probability, πa,b(i)^, from state a to state ba,b∈{1,…,K}, for that trial was calculated by(4)πa,b(i)^≡na,b(i)∑c=1Kna,c(i).(5)na,b(i)≡∑t=1T(i)−1I(zt^=a)I(zt+1^=b).where Ti is the length of trial i, and I⋅ is an indicator function, returning 1 or 0 when its argument is true or false, respectively.

We used the decoder to either classify experimental condition or mouse identity, in different trials (Figure 6D, E). For decoders trained to classify the trials' experimental condition, we used pooled data across mice. For decoders trained to classify mouse identity, we only used data from the 80:20 odor condition. Data was split into training and test dataset in a stratified fivefold cross-validation manner, ensuring equal proportions of trials of different types in both datasets. The trial type was the combination of left vs. right decision, experimental condition, and mouse identity.

To calculate the statistical significance of decoding accuracies, we performed an iterative shuffle procedure on each fold of the cross-validation. In each shuffle, the training labels that the classifier was trained to decode were shuffled randomly across trials of the training set, and the classifier's accuracy was evaluated on the unshuffled test dataset. This shuffle was performed 100 times to create a shuffle distribution of decoding accuracies for each fold of the cross-validation. From these distributions, we calculated the z-score of decoding accuracy for each class in each cross-validation fold. These z-scores were then averaged across the folds of cross-validation and used to calculate the overall p-value of the decoding accuracy obtained on the original data.

Reviewer #2:

In this study, Smear et al. aim to investigate how mice sample the noisy stimulus information from olfactory plumes such as to navigate towards their source. To this end, they developed a 2AFC task for freely moving mice where the same odor emanates from two lateral sources, at independently controllable concentrations. Mice are required to identify the more intense of the two sources and collect water from reward port located on the side with the higher odor concentration. The authors improve on previous attempts at studying this problem by requiring the mice to commit to their decision at a substantial distance from the odor ports. This forces the mice to assess odor concentration from distal cues rather than via serial sampling of the sources themselves. Interestingly, the authors find that stereo olfaction (comparing concentration across two nostrils) is not required to determine source location from distal cues. Using a series of stimulus conditions, the authors convincingly show that in their paradigm, mice rely on olfactory cues and specifically the relative, not absolute, concentration difference between the two sources.

The relevance of stereo olfaction for airborne odor cues has been long debated. In my opinion, the authors results in principle resolve this debate – stereo comparisons allow finer source localisation near the source, while serial sampling may play a larger role farther away from source. One concern however is that this lack of reliance on stereo sampling may result from the specific task design and the constraints it imposes on the behavior (see concerns).

Further, the authors characterise the sampling behaviors of mice during this task by monitoring respiration (thermistor) as well as nose, head and body positions (video tracking). The authors find a striking, active synchronisation of sniffing and nose (and body) movements that gets selectively recruited during putative investigatory phase of the task i.e. when mice are actively exploring the concentration gradient. The authors do exhaustive analysis to show that such synchronisation is not a default state and the coupling is much weaker during other phases within the same trial. While such coupling of movement and intrinsic rhythms has been proposed previously, to my knowledge this is the first careful characterisation of this phenomenon in freely moving mice. Importantly, the authors results not only confirm the existence of such coupling but also clarify that this synchronisation is an active feature of olfactory navigation. Interestingly however, the authors do not find any significant difference in sampling strategies across different stimulus difficulties (see concerns).

Lastly, the authors use machine learning to parse motion trajectories into identifiable behavioral motifs. With their approach, they find that a range of motifs that are stereotyped across mice and occur in non-random sequences during each trial. Further, a trained decoder can successfully decode mouse identity from the sequences in which these motifs in each animal. While these motif based analysis are well done, the data presented do not seem to make any clear predictions about how these motif sequences would change in different task conditions. The authors do not find any obvious relationship between trial types (difficult versus easy stimuli) and motif sequences and the presented analyses do not add much to the main message of the paper. I therefore lack the imagination to accurately assess the relevance of this portion of the study.

Overall, the study is well executed – the data presented are clear with numerous controls at each step. In my opinion, the evidence provided for lack of need for stereo olfaction for distal source assessment and active synchronisation of sniffing and sampling movements are important contributions to the field of olfaction that warrant publication in eLife. However, I have several conceptual concern about the task design and the interpretations of the results that the authors should clarify prior to publication.

1. My primary concern is about the task design. I commend the authors for the careful control of olfactory stimuli and substantial improvements over previously published odor localisation assays by separating the reward port from the odor source and forcing decisions at locations distant from the source. However, the task design chosen does not really require the mice to localize odor sources beyond just indicating whether there is more odor on the right versus left. This is different from natural conditions, where the necessary spatial resolution may be much higher. In fact, finer source localization confers no additional benefit for maximizing reward in this task. Therefore, the sampling strategies exhibited by the subjects here may be different from those employed during natural odor navigation where the motivation is to precisely locate the source of mate, food or predators.

2. Along the same lines, it is surprising that even for the easiest version of the task, the performance hovers around 80%, even though PID characterisations show very clear differences between the two halves of the arena. Furthermore, performance drops with increasing stimulus difficulty but mice do not appear to change their sampling strategies to compensate for the lower reward rate. I am trying to reconcile these two facts. At first pass, given known olfactory acuity of rodents, it seems that trained mice should have no trouble handling the easiest stimuli (reach almost 100% success). One possibility is that the mice are not fully motivated/engaged in the task. An alternate explanation is that mice are fully motivated to reach maximum reward rate, but the task is just too hard and the sampling strategies employed at 100:0 condition are their best, and therefore with increasing stimulus difficulty, they cannot perform any better. Yet, the latter possibility appears very unlikely. Can the authors comment on these two possibilities? The question remains whether mice when pushed to achieve higher performances would employ different sampling strategies.

3. Lastly, looking at Figure 5Ai it appears that overall nose speeds are significantly lower during ITI than during the investigatory bouts within the trial. While the authors rule out that sniffing-movement synchronisation is simply a feature of rapid sniffing, they do not rule out the dependence on running speeds. Perhaps the apparent lack of synchrony in ITI results from poorer ability to resolve decelerations, given lower speeds on average. This is also consistent with reduced, but significant synchrony during premature initiations in the ITI (Figure S7A) where speeds tend to be higher than those shown in Figure 5Ai. This should be easily addressable by repeating the analysis on speed matched datasets.

Reviewer #3:

In this manuscript, Findley and colleagues propose a novel assay to study the behavioral strategy freely moving mice adopt to navigate turbulent odor gradients. This assay is neat and well-thought. It sheds light into the control of active sampling through sniffing and search patterns involving head and body movements. The work is an admirable technical tour de force. The results are built on solid data analysis, which makes use of unsurprised machine learning to avoid subjective biases in the categorization of behavioral states. The manuscript offers a wealth of data that should be a wide interest to the field of olfaction. Finally, the conclusions are presented in a way that is balanced and supported by the well-controlled experimental data. This manuscript combines innovation with rigor to advance our understanding of olfaction in rodents (and beyond).

I have a few suggestions to improve the manuscript. These suggestions do not require any additional experiments.

1. An exciting finding of the manuscript is the description of two behavioral states underlying odor search: investigation and approach. The authors might want to push the analysis of the search strategy one step further by defining whether/how mice can switch from investigation to approach, back to investigation to perform error correction. This process would rule out that animals find the gradient through an initial guess that leads to a full commitment to one side during the approach phase. The data suggests that error correction takes place (Figure 7C and D), but those cases are not analyzed in detail. Can a statistical analysis of the state transitions reveal any principles in the organization of error correction? Does the animal's state indeed switch from approach to investigation during error correction?

2. The occupancy diagram of Figure 3F is fascinating. Together with panel 3D, it suggests that mice undergo fairly stereotyped searches: after poking their nose out of the initiation port, they appear to make a 180 degree rotation (sweep) to face the gradient. The density reaches a maximum at that point (opposite to the position of the initiation port). Is this position (crossing of the alpha shape) dominated by an "investigation" state? Can this position be viewed as a decision point? When/where does the animal tend switch to the "approach" state? More generally, could you map dominate trends in behavioral motifs of Figure 6B onto the stereotyped alpha shape of the occupancy diagram of Figure 3F?

3. Figure 2D: Could you speculate about the reason why trials tend to be longer for the 100:0 conditions compared to the more difficult 60:40? Do mice spend more time in the investigation phase when gradient is stronger? Although this result would be counter-intuitive, it might suggest that mice learn (?) to spend less time on the initial search when less information is available to them.

4. Figure 1D indicates that the average gradient's geometry is not the same when the odor is delivered on the left side (100:0) compared to the right side (0:100). This observation appears to be true for the other odor ratios reported in Figure S2. This asymmetry should affect the gradient that the animal experiences during the investigation phase, which should in turn influence the accuracy of the decisions. Do you expect a 50:50 condition to produce no preference (on average)?

5. Figure 7F: What are you concluding from this panel? Are you sure that the shaded areas represent the standard deviation and not the SEM? If the standard deviation is shown, how do you explain the existence of stereotypical wiggles on a timescale of 50 ms? It would be very useful to represent a variant of Figure 7C where the trials are sorted between correct and incorrect.

results.result: Mice use concentration gradient cues, not absolute concentration or stereo olfaction, to navigate turbulent odor plumes. Performance degrades with shallower gradients but is unaffected by absolute concentration changes at fixed gradients. Naris occlusion does not impair performance, indicating temporal comparisons across sniffs are more important than stereo comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13, C16-18, C21-22 provide converging experimental evidence from gradient manipulation (C13, C16), absolute concentration manipulation (C16-17), and naris occlusion (C18, C21) experiments. Statistical tests support each finding (Wilcoxon rank-sum, binomial tests with appropriate p-values). The inference that temporal comparisons dominate (C22) is well-supported by the naris occlusion results and cited literature.

results.result: During olfactory search, mice synchronize three-dimensional head movements (nose speed, yaw velocity, Z-velocity) with sniffing at tens of milliseconds precision. This synchronization is demonstrated through kinematic analysis aligned to the sniff cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C34-36 describe specific kinematic patterns aligned to sniff phases, supported by data in Figure 5. Permutation testing (C37, p<0.001) confirms these patterns exceed chance. Cross-correlation and coherence analysis further validate synchrony. The temporal precision claim is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Sniff-synchronized movement is a strategic behavioral state selectively deployed during task performance, not a reflexive accompaniment to fast breathing. Synchrony is present during trials but largely absent during inter-trial intervals, even when controlling for movement speed. Mice also show synchrony during premature trial initiations and lose synchrony after decision commitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C39-42 demonstrate context-dependent deployment through trial vs. ITI comparisons with appropriate controls for movement speed (C42). Claims C44-45 provide additional evidence from premature initiations and post-decision periods. The inference that this represents strategic deployment (C43, C46) is well-supported by the pattern of results across multiple behavioral contexts.

results.result: Movement motifs cluster into two behavioral states—investigation and approach—with distinct temporal, kinematic, and sniffing properties. Investigation occurs early in trials with slower movement and faster sniffing, while approach occurs later with faster movement and slower sniffing. Frequent switches between states suggest continuous evidence integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C59-61 describe the two-state structure supported by clustering analysis (Figure 7A) and temporal analysis (Figure 7B-D). Claims C64-66 characterize state-specific properties with statistical support (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<0.01). Permutation testing (C67-68) confirms differences exceed chance for nose speed and yaw velocity. The inference about continuous integration (C63) is reasonable given frequent state switches (C62).

results.result: Investigation motif onsets are precisely locked to specific phases of the sniff cycle, with significant modulation in both time and phase coordinates. This synchronization is consistent across mice, though the data are inconclusive about whether organization is primarily in time versus phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C72-74 describe motif-sniff synchronization supported by peristimulus time histograms (Figure 8B-D). Claims C75-77 provide statistical support through modulation index analysis with permutation testing (p<0.001 for investigation motifs). The acknowledgment of inconclusiveness (C78) regarding time vs. phase organization is appropriate given mixed modulation index results. Overall conclusion (C79) is well-supported.

results.result: Correct trials show increased investigation at and across the midline where gradients are steepest, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy. Investigation downwind of odor ports (where absolute concentration is most discriminable) is associated with incorrect trials, arguing against a single-sniff absolute concentration strategy.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-95 establish theoretical predictions for different strategies based on PID measurements. Claims C102, C104-106 show occupancy patterns consistent with serial-sniff strategy, with statistical support (permutation test, p<0.001, n=9). Analysis of stay vs. switch trials (C112-113) rules out confounds. The inference favoring serial-sniff strategy (C6, C111, C114, C129, C136) is well-supported by converging evidence from spatial occupancy patterns and discriminability analysis.

results.result: AR-HMM modeling identifies recurring movement motifs that capture common features across mice while preserving individual differences. Mouse identity can be decoded from motif sequences with above-chance accuracy (8/9 mice, p<0.01), demonstrating that individual mice have characteristic ways of sequencing motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-49 describe the AR-HMM approach and resulting motifs, supported by model fits and cross-validation (C48, Figure 6—supplement 1). Claims C51-54 demonstrate individual differences through decoding analysis with appropriate statistical testing. The model's ability to capture both common features and individual differences (C121, C162) is well-demonstrated. Acknowledgment of variability (C50) is appropriate.

results.result: Movement sequences are not distinguishable across different concentration ratios (except for odor omission trials), suggesting mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner in the measured movement parameters. The authors speculate this may be due to impulsivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-56 report negative results from decoding analysis, appropriately noting the exception for 0:0 trials. The inference (C57) is cautiously stated as limited to measured parameters. The speculation about impulsivity (C58) is clearly marked as such and supported by citations. The negative result is meaningful given the model's sensitivity to decode mouse identity (demonstrated in other claims).

results.result: Mice rapidly learn the olfactory search task, with most performing above chance in the first session (24/25 mice, 75±9.2% correct) and exceeding 80% performance within four sessions (19/26 mice). The behavior generalizes to novel odorants (vanillin) and does not require trigeminal chemosensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-8 report training performance with appropriate statistical tests (binomial test, p<0.05) and sample sizes. Claim C9 demonstrates generalization with statistical comparison (Wilcoxon rank-sum, p=0.827, n=3). The inference about trigeminal chemosensation (C10) is supported by equal performance with vanillin (which lacks trigeminal activation) and appropriate citations. Small sample size for vanillin experiment (n=3) is a limitation but the result is clear.

results.result: On odor omission probe trials (0:0), mice perform at chance level with longer trial durations, more tortuous trajectories, and altered sampling behavior (more fast sniffing and head turns) compared to odor-present trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-12 report control experiment results with appropriate statistical tests (binomial test for chance performance, Wilcoxon rank-sum for duration and tortuosity, p<0.05). Claim C33 describes altered sampling behavior. These results appropriately validate that behavior is odor-guided and provide insight into search behavior in the absence of odor cues.

results.result: Sniffing and movement patterns during task performance show consistent structure: rapid sniff bursts after trial initiation, slower sniffing during approach, with sniff durations shorter than in head-fixed rodents. Movement trajectories are variable across trials, with individual position biases that average out across mice. Sniff rate is highest near initiation and slower near targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-27 describe temporal sniffing patterns supported by Figure 3A with statistical comparison to ITI (C25, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<<0.01). Comparison to head-fixed data (C26) is supported by citations. Claims C28-31 describe spatial patterns supported by occupancy and sniff rate mapping (Figure 3D-G). Claim C32 notes lack of differences across conditions, which is appropriate given the data.

results.result: Trial duration and path tortuosity show subtle differences across conditions: no difference between 80:20 and 60:40, but slightly longer in 100:0 condition. Naris occlusion causes slight increase in trial duration compared to no-stitch but not compared to sham, suggesting surgical procedure effects rather than occlusion effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-15 report behavioral metrics with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank-sum, p<0.05). Claims C19-20 demonstrate proper use of sham controls to distinguish surgical effects from occlusion effects. The inference about surgical procedure effects (C20) is well-supported by the pattern of results. These are minor findings that support the main conclusions about gradient-guided search.

results.result: Investigation and approach states show distinct spatial distributions: investigation near initiation port, approach near decision line, with overlap in a transition zone (5-10 cm from initiation). When trials are oriented by choice, the overlap region is displaced toward the chosen side, indicating mice primarily switch states while on the side they will ultimately choose.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-87 describe aggregate occupancy patterns supported by Figure 9A. Claims C88-89 reveal individual differences and choice-dependent patterns through reorientation analysis (Figure 9—supplement 1). The inference about state switching location (C90) is well-supported by the choice-oriented analysis. Claims C91-93 characterize the transition zone and lateral distributions. The spatial analysis is thorough and appropriately controlled.

results.result: Correct and incorrect trials show qualitatively similar occupancy maps but differ in investigation-approach index: correct trials show more investigation in the transition zone and less near the decision line. Investigation near the decision line (where absolute concentration is most discriminable) is associated with incorrect trials, suggesting mice cannot capitalize on this cue.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-98 describe correct vs. incorrect differences with statistical support (permutation test, p<0.001, n=9). Claims C99-101 interpret the pattern relative to absolute concentration discriminability (Figure 1—supplement 2C). Claims C107-110 describe approach occupancy patterns. The inference that location matters more than state per se (C99) is well-supported. The interpretation regarding absolute concentration (C101) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Movement trajectories are highly variable across trials, and approach is not a ballistic commitment (frequent switches back to investigation occur). The spatial dependence of investigation effectiveness indicates that sampling location matters for performance, with mice performing best when investigating where gradients are steepest rather than where absolute concentrations are most discriminable.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 describes trajectory variability supported by Figure 3D-E. Claim C123 notes non-ballistic approach supported by state transition analysis (Figure 7C-D). Claims C125-127 interpret the spatial patterns, with C128 inferring that absolute concentration is not used. Claim C130 connects to broader principles with appropriate citation. The inferences are well-supported by the occupancy analysis, though some are interpretive.

results.result: State transitions between investigation and approach mark behavioral inflection points that can be identified across trials and may represent key decision moments. This analysis framework can be used to align diverse movement trajectories with neural recordings, providing a template for studying neural mechanisms of active sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-70 interpret state transitions as decision points, which is reasonable given their temporal structure. Claims C71, C82-84, C166-167 propose utility for future neural studies. These are primarily methodological contributions and interpretive frameworks rather than direct experimental findings. The proposals are reasonable given the demonstrated properties of the motif analysis, though they represent future work rather than current results.

results.result: Breathing synchronizes to other motor and brain rhythms (established knowledge), therefore motifs that synchronize with breathing also correlate with neural activity patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 states established knowledge from literature. Claim C81 makes a logical inference from this knowledge combined with the demonstrated sniff-synchronization of motifs. The inference is reasonable but represents a prediction about neural correlates rather than a direct finding. The claim is appropriately framed as an inference.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within existing literature on olfactory navigation across different spatial regimes and species, discusses differences between freely moving and head-fixed conditions (particularly sniff rates), and proposes that the task design forces mice into a serial-sniff comparison regime. The authors argue for complementing head-fixed studies with freely moving paradigms.
results.evaluation: These claims primarily summarize established knowledge from literature (C131-133, C137-138, C146-148, C152-156) with appropriate citations, compare current findings to previous work (C145), and propose interpretations (C139-141, C143-144, C149-150). The comparisons are accurate and the arguments for studying freely moving behavior are well-reasoned. These are primarily discussion/contextualization rather than novel findings.

results.result: The manuscript situates the work within broader principles of active sensing, sensorimotor integration, and comparative ethology. It notes that two-state search strategies are common across phylogeny and that recent computational tools enable rigorous quantification of freely moving behavior.
results.evaluation: These claims primarily establish context through literature review (C152-156, C163-164) and general principles (C157-160). Claim C161 notes methodological advances with appropriate citations. Claim C165 summarizes a finding from the current work. These are appropriate contextualization and framing of the work within broader scientific principles.

results.result: Mice use concentration gradient cues rather than absolute concentration or stereo olfaction to solve the olfactory search task. Performance varies with concentration ratio but not absolute concentration, and naris occlusion does not impair performance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers extensively questioned whether mice truly use gradient sensing versus memorizing absolute concentrations. They noted the variable |C| experiment (Figure 2E) is 'not really conclusive' because 'performance in the first 10 trials is quite low – so its very likely that the animals just learn a new rule.' Reviewers proposed alternative strategies including memorizing expected concentrations (100, 80, 60) and suggested the task design may not definitively distinguish between gradient sensing and absolute concentration learning.

results.result: Respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision during task performance, with nose speed, yaw velocity, and Z-velocity showing specific modulation patterns relative to the sniff cycle.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledged this finding but noted 'sniff-synchronized movement has also been seen in other studies' and questioned 'how the current work advances this understanding.' Reviewer 2 stated 'this is the first careful characterisation of this phenomenon in freely moving mice' and that the results 'not only confirm the existence of such coupling but also clarify that this synchronisation is an active feature of olfactory navigation.' The finding is accepted but its novelty is questioned.

results.result: Sniff-synchronized movement is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals, indicating it is a strategic behavioral state rather than an inevitable accompaniment to fast breathing.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised a critical concern that 'overall nose speeds are significantly lower during ITI than during the investigatory bouts' and that 'the apparent lack of synchrony in ITI results from poorer ability to resolve decelerations, given lower speeds on average.' The reviewer requested speed-matched analysis to rule out this confound. While the authors claim to control for this (C42), the reviewer's concern about the adequacy of this control was not fully addressed.

results.result: AR-HMM analysis identifies discrete movement motifs that cluster into two states (investigation and approach) with distinct temporal and kinematic properties. Individual mice are identifiable by how they sequence motifs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'the motifs don't appear to be particularly crisp, in that they continue to contribute up to 100 motifs' and stated 'it seems to me that the motifs are fuzzy.' Reviewer 2 commented that 'the data presented do not seem to make any clear predictions' and 'I therefore lack the imagination to accurately assess the relevance of this portion of the study.' Reviewers acknowledged the analysis is well-done but questioned its interpretability and utility.

results.result: Movement sequences are not distinguishable across different concentration ratios, suggesting mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 expressed surprise that 'mice do not appear to change their sampling strategies to compensate for the lower reward rate' and questioned whether 'mice are not fully motivated/engaged in the task' or if 'the task is just too hard.' The reviewer asked 'whether mice when pushed to achieve higher performances would employ different sampling strategies.' This finding conflicts with expectations and raises questions about task engagement and interpretation.

results.result: Investigation motifs lock precisely to sniffing, with individual motifs preferentially occurring at specific phases of the sniff cycle, though the data are inconclusive about time versus phase organization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about the sniff-locking of motifs. Reviewer 1 noted 'the motif correlation to stage of trial and to sniffing and nose speed is interesting but maybe not surprising,' suggesting acceptance of the finding while questioning its novelty. The statistical evidence (permutation tests) appears convincing to reviewers.

results.result: Switches from approach back to investigation are common during trials, suggesting mice continuously integrate evidence about the odor gradient and that state transitions mark behavioral inflection points representing decision moments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically requested the authors 'push the analysis of the search strategy one step further by defining whether/how mice can switch from investigation to approach, back to investigation to perform error correction.' The reviewer asked 'Can a statistical analysis of the state transitions reveal any principles in the organization of error correction?' This indicates the reviewers found the current analysis incomplete and wanted more rigorous characterization of these transitions.

results.result: Investigation and approach states have distinct sniff rates, movement speeds, and sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms, with investigation featuring slower movement, faster sniffing, and stronger synchronization of nose speed and yaw velocity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about these state-dependent differences. The statistical comparisons (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, permutation tests) appear to satisfy reviewers. This finding supports the broader two-state framework that reviewers found interesting.

results.result: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient (at the midline), consistent with a serial-sniff strategy. Correct trials feature increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline where gradients are steepest, while investigation downwind (where absolute concentration is most discriminable) is associated with incorrect trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers extensively discussed alternative decision strategies and questioned the interpretation. One reviewer proposed that 'the mouse could already detect whether the concentration increases or not' during the initial turn and 'I don't think that a sequence of samples on the left and the right side must be taken.' Another reviewer suggested mice might be 'memorizing expected gradients or absolute concentrations' rather than making L-R comparisons. Reviewer 3 asked about asymmetries in the gradient geometry and whether this affects decisions. The serial-sniff interpretation is challenged by alternative explanations.

results.result: Mice learn the task rapidly, with most performing above chance in the first session and exceeding 80% performance within four sessions, then performing approximately 150 trials daily for months.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 expressed surprise that 'even for the easiest version of the task, the performance hovers around 80%' when 'PID characterisations show very clear differences between the two halves of the arena.' The reviewer questioned whether mice are 'not fully motivated/engaged in the task' or if 'the task is just too hard.' This raises concerns about whether the reported performance levels reflect the animals' true capabilities or limitations in task design or motivation.

results.result: Mice generalize their search behavior to vanillin (a novel odorant that does not activate trigeminal fibers), indicating trigeminal chemosensation is not necessary for task performance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about this control experiment. The finding that performance is equivalent with vanillin and pinene appears accepted as evidence that trigeminal activation is not required.

results.result: On odor omission probe trials, mice perform at chance level with longer trial durations, more tortuous trajectories, and increased fast sniffing and head turns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the odor omission control. This finding appears accepted as evidence that mice require odor cues for above-chance performance.

results.result: Various task parameters (concentration ratio changes, naris occlusion) produce subtle effects on trial duration and tortuosity but do not fundamentally alter sampling behavior as measured by the motif analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these specific findings about trial metrics. The statistical comparisons appear accepted, though the broader interpretation about lack of adaptive sampling strategies was questioned (see C55-C58).

results.result: Mice exhibit consistent sniff patterns across trials with rapid bursts of sniffing during investigation, slower sniffing during approach, and non-stereotyped tortuous trajectories. Sniff durations are strikingly shorter than in head-fixed rodents.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these descriptive findings without specific criticism. Reviewer 1 noted 'the detailed characterization of sniffing and its relation to movement' as an accomplishment. The comparison to head-fixed conditions is accepted as highlighting important differences in freely moving behavior.

comparisons.comparison: Both address gradient sensing claims (C1, C13, C16-18, C21-22, C116-117, C135). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED with converging experimental evidence from multiple manipulations. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, extensively questioning whether mice truly use gradient sensing versus memorizing absolute concentrations, noting the variable |C| experiment is 'not really conclusive' and proposing alternative learning strategies.

Both evaluate sniff-synchronized movement claims (C2, C34-38, C151). Both rate SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence (permutation tests, p<0.001). Peer reviewers acknowledge the finding but question its novelty, noting 'sniff-synchronized movement has also been seen in other studies' while recognizing this as 'the first careful characterisation' in freely moving mice.

Both address context-dependent deployment claims (C3, C39-46). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on trial vs. ITI comparisons with speed controls. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising critical concern that 'overall nose speeds are significantly lower during ITI' and that speed-matching controls may be inadequate, requesting additional analysis to rule out this confound.

Both evaluate AR-HMM motif analysis (C47-54, C121-122, C162). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting model validation and ability to capture individual differences. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'the motifs don't appear to be particularly crisp' and 'the data presented do not seem to make any clear predictions,' questioning interpretability and utility despite acknowledging the analysis is well-done.

Both address negative decoding results for trial difficulty (C55-58). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting the negative result is meaningful given model sensitivity. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing surprise that 'mice do not appear to change their sampling strategies' and questioning whether mice are 'not fully motivated/engaged' or if 'the task is just too hard.'

Both evaluate sniff-locking of motifs (C5, C72-79). Both rate SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence (permutation tests, p<0.001). Peer reviewers note the finding is 'interesting but maybe not surprising,' accepting the evidence while questioning novelty. OpenEval appropriately acknowledges inconclusiveness regarding time vs. phase organization (C78).

Both address state transitions as decision points (C69-70, C83-84). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, viewing these as reasonable interpretations and methodological contributions for future neural studies. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, specifically requesting authors 'push the analysis one step further' to define principles of state transitions and error correction, finding the current analysis incomplete.

Both evaluate state-specific kinematic properties (C64-68). Both rate SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, permutation tests, p<0.01). Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about these differences, accepting the evidence for distinct investigation and approach states.

Both address serial-sniff strategy and spatial occupancy patterns (C6, C94-95, C102-106, C111-114, C129, C136). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on occupancy patterns and discriminability analysis with permutation tests (p<0.001). Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, extensively discussing alternative decision strategies including detecting concentration changes during initial turns and memorizing expected concentrations rather than making L-R comparisons.

Both evaluate training performance and task engagement (C7-8, C115). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical tests. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing surprise that 'even for the easiest version of the task, the performance hovers around 80%' when PID measurements show clear differences, questioning whether mice are fully motivated or if the task is too hard.

Both address vanillin generalization control (C9-10). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes small sample size (n=3) but clear result. Peer reviewers accept this as evidence that trigeminal activation is not required, raising no specific concerns about the control experiment.

Both evaluate odor omission control (C11-12, C33). Both rate SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical tests showing chance performance without odor. Peer reviewers accept this as evidence that mice require odor cues for above-chance performance, raising no concerns.

Both address trial metrics and surgical controls (C14-15, C19-20, C32). Both rate SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical comparisons. Peer reviewers accept these specific findings about trial metrics, though they questioned broader interpretations about adaptive sampling strategies in other contexts.

Both evaluate temporal and spatial sniffing patterns (C23-31, C120, C145). Both rate SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'the detailed characterization of sniffing and its relation to movement' as an accomplishment and accept the comparison to head-fixed conditions as highlighting important differences in freely moving behavior.

Both address aggregate occupancy patterns and spatial distributions (C85-93). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on thorough spatial analysis. These claims overlap with peer R9 which rates UNCERTAIN, where reviewers questioned the interpretation of spatial patterns and proposed alternative decision strategies including detecting concentration changes without sequential L-R sampling.

Both evaluate correct vs. incorrect trial differences and location-dependent patterns (C96-101, C107-110). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with permutation tests (p<0.001). These claims overlap with peer R9 which rates UNCERTAIN, where reviewers questioned whether location matters due to gradient geometry asymmetries and proposed alternative explanations for spatial patterns.

Both address trajectory variability and spatial pattern interpretations (C120, C123-128, C130). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, inferring that absolute concentration is not used based on occupancy analysis. These claims overlap with peer R9 which rates UNCERTAIN, where reviewers proposed mice might be memorizing expected concentrations and questioned the interpretation of spatial patterns.

Partial overlap on two-state structure claims (C4, C59-61). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on clustering and temporal analysis. Peer R4 rates UNCERTAIN, focusing on AR-HMM motif analysis (C47-54) and questioning motif crispness and interpretability, though not specifically challenging the two-state characterization.

Partial overlap on state switching and continuous integration (C62-63). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting frequent state switches support continuous integration inference. Peer R7 rates UNCERTAIN, requesting more rigorous statistical analysis of state transitions to reveal principles of error correction organization.

OpenEval R17 addresses neural correlates inference (C80-81), rating SUPPORTED as reasonable prediction based on sniff-synchronization and established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval R18 addresses literature contextualization and comparison to previous work (C131-150), rating SUPPORTED as appropriate framing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer R14 briefly mentions C145 regarding freely moving vs. head-fixed comparisons.

OpenEval R19 addresses broader scientific context and methodological advances (C152-165), rating SUPPORTED as appropriate contextualization. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these discussion/framing claims.
